text:
Scaling an AI agent isn't a discovery problem. It's an interface problem.

I've spent the last month benchmarking Model Context Protocol (MCP) against custom, encapsulated Skills.

MCP is the USB-C of the agent world. It’s clean. It’s standardized. It lets models talk to any data source without writing custom glue code for every project.

But standardization has a ceiling.

When you need an agent to actually perform complex engineering—like migrating a legacy repo or self-healing a CI pipeline—standardized tool definitions aren't enough.

You need Skills.

MCP gives the model a map. A Skill gives the model a manual.

One defines the "what" (the API endpoint). The other defines the "how" (the multi-step cognitive workflow).

The mistake I see most teams making is choosing one and calling it an architecture.

A stack full of MCP servers is just a well-equipped library. Without specialized logic, the model still has to invent a strategy from scratch every time.

That's where the cost spikes and the reliability drops.

Build with MCP for breadth. Build Skills for depth.

Access without intent is just a powerful engine without a driver!\n
How are you drawing the line between generic tool calling and hard-coded cognitive logic in your stack?

#AIEngineering #LLMs #MCP
idea_source: MCP vs SKILLS — two paradigms for extending AI agents
